overview:
On 17 July 1936 a group of Spanish generals, Emilio Mola and Francisco Franco among them, launched a coup against the elected Republic. It half-succeeded, which was the worst possible outcome: the rising took hold in Morocco, Navarre, Old Castile and parts of Andalusia, but failed in Madrid, Barcelona, Valencia and the industrial north, where workers' organisations armed themselves and put it down. What was meant to be a swift seizure of power became a war of fronts. Franco's Army of Africa was ferried across the strait with German and Italian transport aircraft and drove north, detouring to relieve the besieged Alcázar at Toledo before reaching the outskirts of Madrid in November 1936, where the Republic held — the phrase "No pasarán" dates from those weeks. The city would stay under siege for nearly two and a half years. The battles that followed traced the same pattern again and again: Nationalist offensives to cut the Republic in pieces, Republican counter-offensives at Jarama, Guadalajara, Brunete, Belchite and Teruel that bought time at ruinous cost. The last of them, the crossing of the Ebro in July 1938, ended in a four-month grinding battle that destroyed the Republican army's remaining strength. Catalonia fell in early 1939, Madrid at the end of March.

The war was never only Spanish. Britain and France pushed a Non-Intervention Agreement signed by more than two dozen states in August 1936, and a committee sat in London to police it while Germany, Italy and the Soviet Union — all signatories — supplied the belligerents openly. The American ambassador Claude Bowers called the arrangement a dishonest farce. Italy sent tens of thousands of ground troops; Germany sent the Condor Legion, whose bombing of the Basque market town of Guernica on 26 April 1937 became the war's defining image, partly through Picasso's canvas and partly because it demonstrated to a watching Europe what aircraft could do to a town. The Soviet Union sold arms and advisers to the Republic and, through the Comintern, organised the International Brigades — something like 35,000 to 40,000 volunteers from more than fifty countries. The effect of non-intervention was to leave the Republic dependent on a single distant supplier while its enemy drew on two neighbours.

Beneath the fronts ran a second, uglier war. Both sides killed prisoners and political enemies behind their own lines: the Republican rearguard produced the Paracuellos killings outside Madrid in late 1936 and the murder of several thousand clergy, while the Nationalists carried out systematic executions in every district they took and continued them for years after victory. The Republic was also at war with itself. In the summer of 1936 an anarchist-led social revolution had taken over factories and land across Catalonia and Aragón; by May 1937 the Communists and the government wanted the state rebuilt and the revolution wound up, and the collision produced days of street fighting in Barcelona, followed by the banning of the POUM and the fall of Prime Minister Largo Caballero. George Orwell was there and wrote the episode into Homage to Catalonia. Franco's victory in April 1939 sent perhaps half a million people over the French border into camps and exile; some who stayed in France were later deported to Mauthausen. His dictatorship lasted until 1975.
significance: More than any other event of the 1930s, the Spanish war fixed the decade's shape in the minds of the people living through it: a rehearsal in which the democracies chose not to act, the fascist powers learned that they could, and Stalin discovered how little the Western states would do in concert. It gave the world Guernica as a word for the deliberate bombing of civilians, and the International Brigades as the century's most durable image of volunteering for someone else's cause. Militarily, Spain was a laboratory for aircraft, armour and the tactics that would be used across Europe within months of Franco's victory. Politically, it left a dictatorship that outlived Hitler and Mussolini by thirty years, and a settlement of silence that Spain has still not finished undoing — mass graves are being opened and identified today, and the argument over what to call the war and who is owed what remains live in Spanish public life.
coverage: Written from standard reference accounts (Britannica, Wikipedia, the USHMM's Holocaust Encyclopedia) plus a survey of the historiographical dispute over victim numbers; the dataset's 53 events are heavily weighted toward set-piece battles and sieges on the main fronts, so the war in the rearguard, the collectivisations, the naval and colonial dimensions, and the exodus of 1939 are barely represented as mappable points. Casualty figures should be treated as estimates rather than counts: totals of 500,000 and sometimes higher circulate, breakdowns between combat deaths and killings behind the lines vary widely, and the specifically political killings have been argued over for sixty years with figures for Nationalist repression ranging from 40,000 to 200,000 depending on the scholar, the period counted, and often the politics. Franco-era documentation was compiled to serve the regime, provincial records are incomplete, and much of what is now known comes from exhumations begun only after 2000.
